title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the record to the paragraph

questions.prompt: Not one of these notes on a stage designer carries a year. Put them in the order in which they must have happened.

options.text: left the workshop to teach design at the academy
was born in a village above Tabarka
wrote the handbook for the students of his own class
took a job painting scenery in a small workshop
learned to draw from his father, a house painter

questions.explanation: Dates are not the only thing that fixes a sequence: the notes themselves say which one has to come first. A birth opens any life, and a child taught by his father is being taught before he is paid by anybody. Then the two notes that mention the workshop lock together in one direction only, since a man cannot leave a place he has not yet joined. The last one is the subtlest: the handbook was written for the students of a class of his own, so it cannot have been written before he had one to teach. Notes for a biography are normally filed in this order already — when they are not, you rebuild it before you write a word.

questions.prompt: Two notes stand one under the other: "1958 — took over the family printing shop" · "1961 — wrote his first play". Which sentence joins them without claiming more than the notes say?

options.text: Before he took over the family printing shop in 1958, he wrote his first play.
In 1958 he took over the family printing shop, but three years later he wrote his first play.
In 1958 he took over the family printing shop, and three years later he wrote his first play.
Because he took over the family printing shop in 1958, he wrote his first play three years later.

questions.explanation: Both notes are true, they are three years apart, and that is the whole of what is known — so the linker that only says both things happened is the only honest one available. Turning the join into a contradiction announces that a man who runs a printing shop would not be expected to write a play, which nobody has written down. Turning it into a cause is worse, because it makes the shop the reason for the play. And putting the play first flatly contradicts the two years printed in front of you.

questions.prompt: Your dictionary prints, inside the entry for one verb: "head for / towards sth — to move in the direction of". A pupil then writes: "The crowd was heading the ruins." What has he failed to take from the entry?

options.text: the tense in which this verb has to be written out
the meaning the entry gives to this verb here
the spelling this verb takes in its -ing form
the little word that must come before the place

questions.explanation: An entry does not only translate a word, it shows how the word behaves, and the tiny example beside it is where that information hides. Two prepositions are printed there for a reason: this verb cannot reach its destination on its own, and dropping them leaves a sentence English will not accept. The pupil has understood the meaning perfectly — moving towards a place is exactly what his crowd is doing — and he has spelt the form correctly and chosen a tense that suits a scene under way. His whole mistake fits into three letters he did not copy.

questions.prompt: A festival programme credits four things under each show. Which of them names the person who invented the dances?

options.text: the choreography of the show
the text of the evening's play
the troupe named on the page
the venue of the performance

questions.explanation: Choreography is the art of inventing the steps of a dance, so the name printed beside that credit is the name of the person who designed the movement. The text belongs to the writer of the play, whom English calls a playwright or a dramatist; the troupe is the whole group who perform, dancers included, so it names nobody in particular; and the venue is a place, which credits no person at all. Programmes credit by job, and reading them is largely a matter of knowing which job each word stands for.

questions.prompt: Four pupils have written the first line of the same biography. Only one of them opens it the way a first line should. Which one?

options.text: Leïla Mansour was born in 1928, in a town that had no company at all.
Leïla Mansour is a name that most people in this country have met before.
Leïla Mansour, born in 1928, was the first woman to run a national company.
Leïla Mansour did a great many things, and her life is worth reading about.

questions.explanation: One line here says both of the things a first line owes its reader: who she was, and what she did that nobody had done before. The date has not been thrown away either — it has simply been folded in, so that the sentence can open on the woman rather than on a year. Beginning with the birth alone gives the reader a date and no reason to go further. Telling him that the name is well known says nothing about the person carrying it, and telling him that a life is worth reading about is an instruction rather than a reason: a first line has to earn that judgement, not ask for it.

questions.prompt: A newspaper's travel page runs a weekly section headed CYBERTRIPS. What does a reader find in it?

options.text: journeys made by the staff of the big computer firms
journeys explored or prepared without leaving a screen
journeys written up afterwards on a traveller's blog
journeys spent hunting for an internet café in each town

questions.explanation: The word is built out of two pieces, and the first of them points at the internet rather than at any particular trade, page or shop. A cybertrip is a journey you take, or at least prepare, through a screen: you visit the festival's pages, read its programme and choose your evening before you have moved a metre. The section exists because that is now how most travelling begins. Nothing in the word restricts it to people who work with computers; a journey written up once it is over is a report rather than a preparation; and looking for a café with a connection after you have arrived is the very opposite of settling everything at home before you leave.
